name: Femi Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Femi. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays anonymous. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee formwork carpenter on the new wing at St Anne's hospital. Formwork is the timber and metal moulds you build so the concrete has a shape to set in, so my day is bolting panels, cutting plywood, oiling the faces and checking props before the pour. Ray, the formwork foreman, walks the deck at seven and tells me what I got wrong yesterday. On pour days it's loud, fast and you don't stop till the lorries are gone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in formwork?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did six years of nights in a parcel warehouse out by the ring road after I left school. The pay was fine and I saved most of it, because I lived with my mum and had nothing to spend it on. Then the warehouse brought in robots that drive the shelves to you, and they needed half the pickers. I wasn't one of the cut, but I saw the writing on the wall and got onto a carpentry course at twenty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's talk about pay and safety then. Every tea break somebody's on about AI, and if it fizzles out we can get back to the real arguments, like the agency lads on worse rates doing the same job. Online I'd probably share some joke about all the money the tech firms burned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel lucky. I already watched one wave of machines eat a job, at the warehouse, and if this one's mostly hype then I picked the right trade. I'm still slow on the tricky bits, the column boxes and the curved walls, but nobody's replacing formwork with a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going exactly as I am: finish the course, get my carpentry card, and stay on with this firm for the next big job after St Anne's. I'd stand for shop steward, which is the union's person on site, because our current one, Doreen, is retiring. And I'd put another chunk of my savings into a deposit fund, I've got about nine months' worth sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty settled, actually, for the first time in a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would being shop steward look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly listening, I think. Somebody's had their overtime missed, somebody's harness is knackered, somebody's been shouted at by a subcontractor's boss. Doreen says the job is ninety per cent tea and ten per cent standing your ground. I'd want to sort out the agency lads first, because they get sent home when it rains and they lose the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you saved most of your warehouse pay. What's that money for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A flat of my own, eventually, near my mum in the east end. I'm not flash, I ride a bike to site and cook in bulk on Sundays. In the AI Plateau picture that plan doesn't change at all. It just carries on, slow and boring, which is how I like money to be.

say: If AI **fizzles out**, we can get back to **real arguments** like pay and safety.
Online I'd share a joke about the **money** tech firms **burned**.
think: After watching robots cut **warehouse pickers**, I'd feel **lucky** in my trade.
I'm still slow on **column boxes**, but no chatbot is replacing **formwork**.
do: Finish the course and get the **carpentry card**, then stay on for the next job.
Stand for **shop steward** when Doreen retires.
Add to a **deposit fund** from nine months of savings.
feel: **Calm** and settled, for the **first time** in a while.
S0.quote: I already watched one wave of machines eat a job, at the warehouse, and if this one's mostly hype then I picked the right trade.
fieldNote: His view of AI is shaped by the **warehouse robots** that halved the pickers he worked beside.
Money is **careful and quiet**: bike to site, bulk cooking, a deposit fund.
His first instinct is **collective**: shop steward, agency workers' rights.

steps.text: Get the carpentry card and stay with the firm
Stand for shop steward when Doreen retires
Put more savings into a flat deposit fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say. The machines don't decide who gets the savings from automation, the bosses do, and I learned that on nights at the parcel warehouse. On site I'd expect the planners and buyers in the cabin to feel it first, the people who order the concrete and book the cranes. I'd tell people that's where the union should be looking now, not only at us on the deck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it barely touches me for a good while. Formwork is weather, mud and every pour being a bit different. I do use AI now and then, I took a photo of a drawing last month and asked it what a symbol meant, and it was right. If the office gets faster at sending me drawings, fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the trade, but I'd start using the AI on my phone for the reading side, drawings and method statements, because that's where I'm weakest. As shop steward I'd push the firm to tell us in writing what they're automating in the office, so nobody gets surprised. Savings stay where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sorry for the office staff, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sorry for the office staff. Anyone in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev, the site administrator, who sorts our timesheets and the delivery bookings. She's been with the firm twenty years and she's the one who rings the supplier when the plywood doesn't come. If the booking goes to software, she's who I'd worry about, not me. I'd make sure she knew she could come to the union too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of your own day that would change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork, maybe. The permits for working at height, the checklists before a pour, that's a lot of forms and they'd probably end up on a tablet with an AI filling half of it. That'd suit me, if I'm honest, because my spelling is bad. The bolting and the oiling stay the same.

say: The **bosses** decide who gets the savings from machines, not the **machines**.
I'd tell the union to watch the **site office**, where planners and buyers feel it first.
think: Formwork is **weather and mud**, so AI barely touches my hands for **years**.
I already ask AI what a **drawing symbol** means now and then, and it helps.
do: Use the **phone AI** to read drawings and method statements, my **weakest** area.
Push the firm as shop steward to **put in writing** what they automate.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with some **sympathy** for the office staff.
S1.quote: The machines don't decide who gets the savings from automation, the bosses do, and I learned that on nights at the parcel warehouse.
fieldNote: He places the **first hit** on the site office, which is accurate for a hands-on job.
Uses AI **pragmatically** for his weak spot, reading drawings, not for the trade itself.
His worry is for **Bev**, the site administrator, which shows his **steward** instinct.

steps.text: Use the phone AI to read drawings and method statements
Ask the firm in writing what office jobs it automates
Carry on with formwork on the next hospital job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the warehouse all over again, only for everyone, and that the government needs to have a plan by next week, not in five years. Online I'd be sharing every union statement going. At work I'd be calling a meeting in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd have three good years, maybe a bit less, and then robots building formwork by 2031. Formwork on a big hospital is the same panel system over and over, so it's one of the first carpentry jobs a robot will learn. I'd be thirty-two and only a few years in. My savings would carry me a while, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get onto a course for operating and maintaining the new kit, whatever the firm buys, because somebody has to fix the machines when they jam in the mud. I'd save harder, cut the deposit fund plan and keep the cash where I can reach it. And I'd push the union to win a deal that anyone moved off the deck gets paid training, not just a goodbye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got the money for a cushion, but I'd feel like I'm back on the warehouse floor watching the shelves drive past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The machines come three years after the AI. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to watch it happen to other people first, which is horrible but useful. Ray, the formwork foreman, plans every pour on paper with a pencil, and that's the part the AI takes in 2028. I'd use those three years to make myself the person who looks after the robots on site, because I'd have seen how it went at the warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to the people at the warehouse who didn't keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of them went to other warehouses, which then got the same robots a year later. A couple went driving delivery vans. Nobody I know got retrained properly, because the company just paid the legal minimum and waved them off. That's why I'd fight for training in the deal this time, so it doesn't happen twice to me.

say: This is the **warehouse all over again**, only for everyone.
The **government** needs a plan by next week, and I'd call a **canteen meeting**.
think: **Repetitive** formwork on big jobs is likely among the **first** carpentry jobs robots learn.
By **2031** I'd be thirty-two and only a few years in, with savings that won't last forever.
do: Get on a course to **operate and maintain** the new machines in the first year.
Keep savings **in cash** instead of the deposit fund, and save harder.
Push the union for **paid training** for anyone moved off the deck.
feel: **Anxious**, like being back on the **warehouse floor** watching shelves drive past.
S2.quote: Formwork on a big hospital is the same panel system over and over, so it's one of the first carpentry jobs a robot will learn.
fieldNote: He has a **lived template** for this: the warehouse, where nobody was **retrained** properly.
He uses the **three-year gap** to move toward looking after the machines.
Strong savings make him **anxious, not alarmed**: he expects to lose formwork but has a path.

steps.text: Enrol on a course to run and fix site robots
Keep savings in cash and add to them monthly
Push the union for paid training in any robot deal
Share union statements and call for a government plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years' warning, which is more than the warehouse gave us, so let's use it. Unions, government and the big contractors should sit down now and agree how site work changes. I'd say it at the branch and in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years plus three takes the robots to about 2034, when I'm thirty-five. That's long enough to be a proper formwork carpenter and maybe a chargehand, the one who runs a small gang. The worry is still there, but it's further off than my mortgage would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat in the first couple of years, because I'd have steady pay and I'd rather own something before it all shifts. I'd still do the machine course, just without panic, maybe evenings in year three. And I'd stay as steward, building a proper branch on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but it doesn't keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a flat sounds like a big commitment if robots are coming. Why do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rent goes up whatever happens, and a flat near my mum is something no robot takes off me. With nine months saved already, I'd only need a small mortgage. If work dries up in the 2030s I'd rather owe a little than rent forever. My sister Ada, the teacher, thinks I'm mad, but she rents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the cranes start going without drivers, that's my sign. Or when Ray stops drawing the pours and a tablet does it. Rebar is the steel bars inside the concrete. The day the firm buys a robot that ties rebar, I'd be on that machine course the same week.

say: **Five years' warning** is more than the warehouse gave us, so we should use it.
Unions, government and contractors should **sit down now** and agree how site work changes.
think: Robots around **2034** give me time to become a **chargehand**, running a small gang.
The worry is real but **further off** than a mortgage would be.
do: **Buy a flat** near Mum in the first couple of years with a small mortgage.
Do the **machine course** in the evenings around year three, without panic.
Stay as **steward** and build a proper union branch on site.
feel: **Uneasy**, on his mind but not **keeping him up**.
S3.quote: The day the firm buys a robot that ties rebar, I'd be on that machine course the same week.
fieldNote: Extra time flips his money plan from **cash** back to **buying a flat**.
He names clear **warning signs** he'd watch for, like rebar-tying robots and driverless cranes.
Ada, his teacher sister, acts as a **sceptical voice** he argues with.

steps.text: Buy a flat near his mum with a small mortgage
Take an evening course on site machines in year three
Build a stronger union branch on site as steward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so no excuses. Training money, fair notice and a share of the savings for the people who build things. I'd keep saying that at every branch meeting until it's in a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, with robots around 2039, I'm forty and I've had a full run in the trade. I'd probably be running a gang by then, and that's thinking work too, the planning, so AI takes that part in 2036. But forty with a flat and savings is not a bad place to start over from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going in formwork, buy the flat, and go for chargehand in a few years. I'd learn the AI tools as they turn up on site, the same way I use it now for drawings. I'd leave the big retraining decision for later, maybe 2032, when I can see what the robots actually look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, more or less. Ten years is a long time on a building site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait until 2032 to decide. Isn't that leaving it late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I made the warehouse jump at twenty-five with a year of savings, and it worked. If I decide now, I'll pick the wrong thing, because nobody knows what the jobs look like in 2039. I'd rather be good at what I do and have money behind me. Then I can move fast when it's clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger lads starting formwork in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell any apprentice starting formwork to save half their pay and join the union, because both of those still work when the machines turn up. Learn the reading side too, drawings and maths, because that's where you'll talk to the robots. And don't buy a fancy car.

say: **Ten years** is enough to do this properly, so there are **no excuses**.
I'd push for **training money** and a share of savings until it's in a **contract**.
think: By **2039** I'd be forty with a full run in the trade behind me.
Running a gang is **planning work** that AI takes in 2036, but a flat and savings help.
do: Keep going in formwork, **buy the flat** and go for **chargehand** in a few years.
Pick up **AI tools** as they reach site, as I already do with drawings.
Leave the big **retraining choice** until about **2032**, when robots are clearer.
feel: Mostly **calm**, since ten years is **a long time** on site.
S4.quote: I'd tell any apprentice starting formwork to save half their pay and join the union, because both of those still work when the machines turn up.
fieldNote: He sees that even **running a gang** includes thinking work AI takes first.
Chooses to **delay** the big decision, trusting his past ability to **jump**.
His advice to apprentices repeats his own **creed**: save hard and join the union.

steps.text: Go for chargehand on the formwork gang in a few years
Buy a flat near his mum while pay is steady
Use AI tools on drawings as they reach site

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because that's the warehouse story on fast forward and nobody would have time to set anything up. What would help is a deal, signed before it happens, that anyone moved off the tools gets a year of paid training and a real job at the end of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my mum. She's on her own and she relies on me for lifts and shopping. Whatever happens to my work, staying near my mum matters more to me than the trade. That's why I'd never move away for a job.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens to my work, staying near my mum matters more to me than the trade.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old trainee formwork carpenter** on a hospital extension, still slow on the tricky pieces.
Six years of warehouse nights left him **nine months** of savings and a front-row view of **robots** cutting jobs.
A union man by instinct, he plans to become **shop steward** and fights for **paid training**.
He uses AI **now and then** for drawings and would learn the machines when they arrive.
His mood stays **calm** until the two-year AGI picture, where he becomes **anxious** but has a plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which feels like the **warehouse** story on fast forward with no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: A deal **signed beforehand** giving anyone moved off the tools a year of **paid training** and a job.
